messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 58-year-old South Asian product manager, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself “small, quiet, and hard to notice” in the ordinary routines of his life. He had been tortured during a period of political detention in his early adulthood, and he described that time as beginning with the sound of boots in a corridor, shouted orders he could not understand, and the sight of uniforms and weapons that made everything feel instantly fatal. What stayed with him most was not only the pain, but the confusion: men barking at him in a language he could not make out, lights flashing, his head spinning from exhaustion and fear, and the sense that his body had become an object other people could overtake at will. In the years since, Ravi had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that there was something about him that had made the torture happen, and that nothing good could happen to him anymore. Those beliefs shaped his days. He avoided anything that could be stressful, steered clear of military or police uniforms or weapons, and kept a close watch on his body for the smallest sign of danger or injury, as if constant checking might give him a chance to prepare before harm found him again.

At work, where he managed product schedules and spent long hours in meetings, Ravi noticed that incomprehensible chatter could make him tense in a way he could not explain to colleagues. When several people spoke over one another in conference rooms or on video calls, he would lose his concentration and feel as if he were back in the detention room, unable to tell what was being demanded of him. Sirens outside his office building or on the commute home were just as unsettling, especially when they cut through an otherwise ordinary afternoon; they seemed to pull him abruptly into the worst moments of his past. Feeling dizzy or lightheaded had become another potent signal, because in his mind it meant his body was failing him and danger was near. He would leave meetings early, avoid crowded transit when he could, and arrange his day so there were as few surprises as possible. Over time, this shrinking of his world made him more convinced that life was no longer safe or open to him. The more he organized himself around avoiding stress and reading his body for threat, the more he interpreted his vigilance as proof that he had reason to be afraid, and the stronger his mistrust of other people became.

Ravi lived in a state of constant readiness. He said he reacted with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, even something as simple as a hand on his shoulder from a coworker or his wife reaching for him in the kitchen. He was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, and at night he woke to check whether he was safe before letting himself drift back toward sleep. Those checks briefly soothed him, but they also kept his attention fixed on danger, so that every small sensation became loaded with meaning. If his heart was racing, if he felt faint, if voices in the hallway sounded blurred or strange, he took it as confirmation that something was wrong. Because he was constantly scanning for signs of injury or attack, his body felt increasingly unreliable, and the very act of monitoring made him more sensitive to dizziness, startle, and the nervous jolt of being touched. He noticed that the more he tried to manage himself this way, the more the world seemed to supply reminders of what he feared.

By the time he sought help, his wife had begun to notice how much he was doing to keep himself from being unsettled, and how little ease remained in him even at home. Ravi was tired of living as if one wrong sound or glance could bring everything back. He feared that if he did not keep avoiding stress, watching his body, and staying alert, he would be caught unprepared again; at the same time, he was increasingly afraid that the life he had built around protection was leaving him with nowhere left to feel safe. What brought him to treatment was the sense that his vigilance had become its own prison, and what he most hoped for was the possibility that he might one day sit through a meeting, hear a siren, or be touched on the arm without immediately bracing for torture.
